1 · ComplianceAre any Basel rules violated?

Every Basel requirement the filings let us compute was tested for all 50 banks in each year, with risk-weighted assets restated under Basel: the card book at 75% (CRE20.68) and unused lines converted at 10% (CRE20.100).

c Filed under the community bank leverage ratio that year, so its risk-based ratios use the project's conservative proxy for risk-weighted assets (9, 8 and 8 banks in FY2023–FY2025). Total capital is a lower bound: Tier 1 plus the allowance that may count as Tier 2 (capped at 1.25% of RWA). The liquidity test uses Basel's 5% retail drawdown (LCR40.64) as a proxy; the LCR does not legally bind U.S. banks of this size.

  • No bank breaks the leverage ratio in any year.
  • Credit First (Brook Park, OH) breaks every capital floor in FY2024 and FY2025, with CET1 of 4.3% and 4.3%. In FY2023 its 4.7% clears the 4.5% minimum but not the 7.0% that the conservation buffer adds. It holds about $39m of assets against $11.4bn of unused card lines: at a 10% conversion factor the lines alone outweigh its capital.
  • DSRM National Bank fails total capital in FY2023: 9.2% against 10.5%. It filed under the community bank leverage ratio that year and reports no allowance that could count as Tier 2. It passes from FY2024.
  • Liquidity is the rule broken most often: 5 banks in FY2023, 6 in FY2024 and 6 in FY2025 cannot cover a 5% drawdown of their unused lines with liquid assets. FY2025: John Deere Financial (0.003×), Credit First (0.064×), DSRM National Bank (0.2×), Credit One Bank (0.5×), TCM Bank (0.6×) and Comenity Bank (0.6×).
  • Capital Bank passes every test in every year. Its narrowest margin is total capital at 12.7% against 10.5% in FY2025; its liquid assets cover a 5% drawdown of its lines 70.4× over.

3 · CompletenessWere any rules missed? Some were, and they are now in place

Before this update, 21 of the 99 branches carried no rule, so in every bank-year between 10 and 16 nodes sat in a bank's tree with nothing to test (2,003 node-years marked “rules pending”). Among them were operational risk, securitisation, Pillar 2, Pillar 3, scope, transitional arrangements, less-stable retail deposits and non-operational wholesale funding.

The final update adds 191 rules, each a paraphrase cited to its paragraph and linked to the BIS text, and moves 53 rules that had been filed where they could never apply: 19 NSFR available-stable-funding rules, 20 large-exposure rules, 5 HQLA composition caps and 5 LCR outflow definitions had been filed under the IRB asset classes, where every rule is out of reach of a standardised-approach bank; 2 public-sector deposit run-offs sat under public-sector loans, and 2 less-stable deposit rules under stable deposits. The 99 nodes are unchanged.

After the update

  • No node is pending in any of the 150 bank-years.
  • Each of the 864 rules sits on exactly one node and receives exactly one disposition in every bank-year.
  • All 2,203 of 2,203 two-way proof checks still pass: the forward counts add back to 99 and 864, and the filing amounts add back to each bank's own totals.
  • Capital Bank, FY2025: 11 evaluated on its own figures, 577 apply, 19 resolve to Basel's default, 26 have no exposure, 12 are out of scope (market risk), 111 are scoped to larger banks, 108 need internal models, which adds back to 864.

Every chapter of the Basel Framework

All 127 chapters of the consolidated framework (BIS structure table, July 2024) were checked against the tree. 45 hold rules; each of the rest has a stated reason: market risk is out of scope, IRB chapters need model approval, two operational-risk chapters were superseded in 2023, glossaries, guidance and supervisor-only principles bind no bank, and template-level Pillar 3 detail cannot be read from a Call Report. The chapter-by-chapter list is in the Rule Atlas under “What changed in the final update”.

Rules that bind but cannot be tested from a Call Report

  • Operational risk (OPE25). Basel adds operational-risk RWA of 12.5 × 12% of the business indicator for every bank here (all are in bucket 1). U.S. standardised-approach RWA carry no operational-risk charge, so every Basel capital ratio above is an upper bound. The business indicator needs income-statement detail that the panel does not hold.
  • Interest rate risk in the banking book (SRP31). The supervisory outlier test, a fall in economic value above 15% of Tier 1 under six prescribed shocks, needs repricing schedules that are not filed.
  • Expected-credit-loss transition (CAP90). A bank using the U.S. CECL transition reports CET1 with part of its allowance added back; CAP90.17 asks for fully loaded ratios as well.
  • Counterparty credit and fund holdings (CRE52, CRE60). Derivative notional appears in 80 bank-years and listed equity securities in 63, but SA-CCR needs replacement cost and add-on inputs, and the fund rules need to know which holdings are funds.

5 · Best practiceWhat the five best banks have in common

  • FY2023: Capital Bank, Lead Bank, 1st Financial Bank USA, WebBank and Credit One Bank
  • FY2024: Capital Bank, Lead Bank, WebBank, 1st Financial Bank USA and Farm Bureau Bank
  • FY2025: Capital Bank, Lead Bank, 1st Financial Bank USA, Merrick Bank and Farm Bureau Bank
  • Lines that customers use. Median utilisation 46% against 7% at the weakest five, and the gap holds in all three years. Basel converts every unused dollar at 10% and weights it at 75% (CRE20.100, CRE20.68), and the liquidity standard expects 5% of it to be drawn in a month (LCR40.64); an unused line costs capital and liquidity and earns nothing.
  • Capital spent on priced regulatory retail. A median 39% of assets in regulatory retail at a 75% weight (weakest five: 14%), with card yields of 26% against 11% and losses of 5.5% against 2.8% absorbed inside the margin.
  • Capital well above the floor. Median Basel CET1 of 20.4%; the lowest of the five is 11.4%, against 7.0% required (RBC20.1, RBC30.2), as SRP20.3 expects.
  • A liquidity buffer sized to the lines. Every best-five bank covers a 5% drawdown of its lines: at least 1.2× in FY2023, 2.7× in FY2024 and 2.9× in FY2025.
  • Recognised collateral. Capital Bank ($96m) and Lead Bank ($434m) carry loans at a 0% risk weight, which only cash collateral or an unconditional guarantee allows (CRE22).
  • One warning, not a practice. 1st Financial Bank USA (78%) and Merrick Bank (79%) fund themselves mostly with brokered deposits, which Basel treats as less stable (LCR40.13) and Pillar 2 asks to diversify (SRP30.49).

  • Gaps that do not hold: corporate lending (the best five hold more of it in FY2024), construction lending and liquidity cover change sign from year to year, so none of them is a practice.
  • In Basel terms, the weakest five put their capital into exposures weighted at 100% (unrated corporates) and 60–150% (commercial real estate and construction) that earn less than card balances weighted at 75%, and leave card lines unused that still attract a 10% conversion factor and a 5% liquidity charge.

7 · A weak bank up closeJohn Deere Financial: which rule it breaks, and how

John Deere Financial (Middleton, WI) ranks 16 of 18 measurable card books in FY2025 with a Basel return of $0.10, and fails the liquidity test in every year (0.003×, 0.003×, 0.003×). Its capital and leverage ratios pass.

  1. Its revolving lines to farm customers are reported as credit-card lines: $33.5bn unused against $539m drawn, so 1.6% of the lines are in use.
  2. Basel treats an unused committed line as a promise the bank must fund in stress. LCR40.64 assumes 5% of committed retail lines is drawn within thirty days: $1.67bn.
  3. The bank holds $5.1m of liquid assets, all of it cash. Cover is 0.003×: the requirement is about 327 times what it holds, a shortfall of $1.67bn.
  4. The same lines weigh on capital: at the 10% conversion factor and 75% weight (CRE20.100, CRE20.68) they add $2.51bn of risk-weighted assets that earn nothing, and its Basel RWA come to 170% of total assets.
  5. The Pillar 2 rules added in this update name the failure directly: liquidity risk from contingent commitments must be identified and controlled SRP30.49, its cost priced into product approval SRP30.50, and stress tests must size the cushion SRP30.51. With 83% of its assets in farm and commercial lending, it is also a sector concentration in the sense of SRP30.20–30.22.

How its distribution differs from the best bank's. John Deere Financial's book is almost all farm and commercial lending with no real estate and almost no liquid securities, and its card lines are nearly all unused. Capital Bank spreads its book across commercial and residential real estate, corporate lending and sovereign exposure, keeps 11.2% of its assets in Level 1 liquid assets and has half of its card lines drawn. In tree terms John Deere Financial's tree is a strict subset of Capital Bank's: of the 80 branches where a bank's own book can differ, 40 are in both trees, 21 only in Capital Bank's and 0 only in John Deere's. The 21 it lacks: Sovereign exposures, Bank exposures, Securities firms and other financial institutions, Subordinated debt, equity and other capital instruments, Real estate exposures, Regulatory residential real estate, Regulatory commercial real estate, Land acquisition, development and construction, Counterparty credit risk and credit derivatives, Credit risk mitigation, Eligible collateral and haircuts, Guarantees and credit derivatives, Securitisation exposures, Level 2A assets, Level 2B assets, Retail deposits — stable · 3–5% run-off, Funding from financial institutions · 100%, Other commitments · 40% CCF, Direct credit substitutes · 100% CCF, Tier 2 and Regulatory adjustments and deductions.

What would bring it into line. Either hold $1.67bn more liquid assets, about 49% of its balance sheet, or cut unused lines to about $102m, which the cash it holds can cover. Two points cut the other way: Basel leaves the drawdown rate for unconditionally cancellable lines to national discretion (LCR40.67), and if these were classed as facilities to farm businesses rather than retail, LCR40.64 would set 10%, doubling the requirement to $3.35bn.

8 · CorrectionsWhat changed from the earlier draft

  • “No rule was missed” was premature: 21 branches had no rules and 53 rules sat where they could not apply. Both are fixed; the tree's 99 nodes are unchanged.
  • Credit First passes the 4.5% CET1 minimum in FY2023 (4.7%); it breaks every capital floor only in FY2024 and FY2025.
  • DSRM National Bank fails total capital with buffer in FY2023 (9.2%), which the earlier draft did not report.
  • Liquidity failures are now reported for every year (5, 6 and 6), not FY2025 alone.
  • The corporate share is not a consistent difference between the best and weakest five: recomputed on gross mapped assets it is 11% against 13% in FY2025 (earlier: 11% against 20%), and the gap reverses in FY2024.
  • Recounted from the tree data, 40 of the 80 branches are in both John Deere Financial's and Capital Bank's trees (earlier: 34); the 21 only in Capital Bank's, and none only in John Deere's, are unchanged.

One bank's Basel tree

The Basel framework is 99 nodes and 864 rules here (673 extracted with verbatim quotes, 191 added in the final update as cited paraphrases). This is the part of it that governs one bank, read from that bank's own Call Report. Every line of the filing is drawn on the right, wired to the node it lands on; every node the bank does not reach stays visible, with the reason it is out.

The diagram is wider than the screen: scroll it sideways.

Two trees over the same framework. Where they overlap the two strands run together; where they do not, each path is kept and drawn in the colour of the bank that holds it. Every path in the union is shown, including the ones neither bank reaches.

The diagram is wider than the screen: scroll it sideways.

Where the two trees part

The map is checked in both directions. Forward, every node and every rule of the framework gets exactly one status for this bank, and the counts add back to 99 and 864. Backward, every line of the bank's filing lands on a node, and the mapped amounts add back to the totals the bank itself reported. Where the two meet, a node is in the tree if and only if evidence lands on it.

Bring in any other bank. Drop its quarterly Call Reports here and this page reads them with the same engine the 50 banks were built with: the bank gets its own tree, its two-way proof, a Basel return and a rank, and joins the comparison, the map and the matrix straight away.

Drop the filings

  • FFIEC XBRL (.xml), one quarter per file, as downloaded for one bank
  • FFIEC text, tab- or semicolon-separated: one item per row, or the bulk “single period” schedule files with one bank per row (add the POR file and names come with them)
  • This project's JSON, the files in bank_filings_2023_2025/

What a bank needs

The 31 December report for each year it should appear in (FY2023 to FY2025). Add the quarters before it too: the ranking averages card balances over five quarter-ends, and with only the December report it uses that one balance.

Download them from the FFIEC Central Data Repository, cdr.ffiec.gov/public: find the bank, then save its Call Report for each quarter.

Checking where added banks can be kept…

Banks added to the panel

Method. The tree is the Basel framework as extracted in outputs/rule_tree.json. Each bank's tree is cut from it by src/analysis/bank_tree.py, which maps every line of the bank's 31 December Call Report onto a node and records why every node and rule is in or out. The decision layer (Basel return, gates, rank) is basel_card_profit_rank.py, unchanged in method, and reproduces the FY2023–FY2025 ranking report to the cent. The final update attaches 191 further rules, each paraphrased and cited to its Basel paragraph, to the branches that had none, moves 53 misfiled rules to the branch they govern, and re-runs every status and proof; the Findings tab sets out the results.

Reading the statuses. In the tree: the filing reports exposure here; or the node applies to every bank; or the bank sits here but no rule has been extracted for the node yet (after the final update no node is left in this state). Default applies: Basel grants this treatment only when a condition is shown, the filing does not show it, so Basel's fallback is used instead, as the ranking does. Out: no exposure, internal-models only, scoped to larger banks, or out of scope.
